# Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] GOV.UK recommends turning research questions into ordered interview topics, starter questions, and possible follow-ups; pilot the structure with a colleague and revise unclear questions or awkward flow before creating the discussion guide. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/

## How it works

- [statement] Balance clarification against interference: silent observation preserves more of the activity’s natural flow but can leave its meaning unclear; occasional questions add understanding, while step-by-step explanation changes how people perform the activity. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Observation may miss rare events because its time window is limited; a critical-incident interview can elicit unusual events outside that window, with the memory and typicality limitations stated above. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/
- [statement] NN/G recommends explicitly transitioning from the introductory interview to watching actual work; agree that the participant can defer interruptions and redirect summaries or grievance lists back to normal work when needed. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Ask for clarification when an observed action is unclear and let participants correct interpretations; reserve final questions for the end so understanding can improve without repeatedly interrupting work. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] If work cannot safely be interrupted, observe with minimal interference and defer clarification questions until an appropriate stopping point or after the session. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Use open, neutral questions and short clarification probes; ask for concrete past episodes instead of inviting agreement with a proposed product or predicting future use. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Discovery interviews investigate users’ circumstances, problems, and existing ways of addressing them; use the conversation to understand their world rather than pitch a proposed product. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Use open, neutral starter questions and short probes for detail; ask participants to explain actions or clarify meaning rather than supply an expected answer. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Ground interviews in specific stories and real examples; asking about the last occurrence, what the person did, and what they previously tried keeps discovery focused on reported past behavior rather than hypothetical product adoption. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] NN/G cautions that retrospective process accounts can omit important reasoning and habitual details, and recommends validating recollections with observation; a past-behavior account should therefore be treated as a report to investigate rather than guaranteed truth. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] NN/G advises using direct observation with later clarification when participants cannot safely be interrupted, and scopes contextual inquiry toward understanding complex work rather than assuming its interview component is always necessary. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Discovery interviews explore users’ circumstances, needs and problems; contextual inquiry combines interviewing with observation while people work in their usual environment. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Keep discovery conversations centered on actual problems, actions and workarounds. Pitching a solution or asking whether someone would use it risks polite agreement being mistaken for evidence. (medium confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/ · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews
- [statement] Contextual inquiry combines observing real activities in the user’s normal environment with questions about how and why the work happens; contextual observation can expose effects of equipment, documents, and distractions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Concrete examples still depend on memory: recalled accounts may lose details, and critical-incident interviews can emphasize extreme events while missing ordinary usage. Do not treat a detailed story as a complete record of behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/ · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Make the transition from conversation to observation explicit. Explain that the participant should continue normal work, how questions will interrupt it and that they may defer an interruption; otherwise they may stay in interview mode. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Record observed actions separately from interpretations, then ask participants to clarify what happened and correct your understanding. A wrap-up provides time to check interpretations without repeatedly interrupting the work. (medium confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Obtain informed consent and explain the session before observation or interviewing; NN/G also calls for confidentiality discussion and approval for recording, while GOV.UK says to reconfirm consent before recording something new. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Actively seek contrary information and avoid communicating a preferred answer: prior beliefs can shape the interviewer’s interpretation, and participants may supply the answers they think the researcher wants. (medium confidence) — https://www.producttalk.org/glossary-discovery-confirmation-bias/ · keywords: Discovery interviews and contextual inquiry for UX · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] NYU recommends looking for existing investments of time or money and workarounds as evidence of a problem; this is practitioner guidance for discovery, not a quantified predictive rule. (low confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
